DP-Puzzle combines shared multi-precision datapaths with precision-specific compute units to tune throughput allocation; we compare nine configurations, jointly modeling area, power, and precision migration. Growing model sizes and computational demands have made lower-precision numerical formats a common optimization for large AI models~. General matrix multiplication (GEMM) increasingly uses TensorFloat-32 (TF32), FP16, and BF16 in place of FP32. Advances in quantization have also made FP8, INT8, FP6, FP4, and microscaling formats~ with shared scaling factors important options for inference. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash~, for example, uses mixed-precision GEMMs: mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and most attention projections use FP8, the QK path of the sparse attention indexer uses MXFP4, and the main attention QK/PV computations use BF16. These workloads require inference hardware to support multiple precisions within the same model.

Recent commercial AI chips depart from this ratio by selectively increasing FP4 throughput or increasing both FP8 and FP4 throughput, as summarized in Table~. Models evolve faster than chips, so a ratio suited to current demand may become inefficient for future workloads. Tensor cores must therefore balance hardware cost against current and future precision demands.

We present DP-Puzzle to connect the hardware cost of throughput-ratio choices to their benefits for evolving model workloads. Tensor cores typically organize dot-product units into two-dimensional arrays with systolic~ or broadcast dataflows. We therefore focus on dot-product units that support multiple formats and allow low-precision throughput to be increased independently. We characterize their area and power using Synopsys synthesis and power analysis at 12\,nm and 1\,GHz, then construct a chip-level throughput model under common area and power constraints. Five precision-migration scenarios represent possible changes in future workloads, allowing us to evaluate the estimated GEMM compute-latency benefits of nine throughput ratios.

We therefore focus on dot-product units that support multiple formats and allow low-precision throughput to be increased independently. We characterize their area and power using Synopsys synthesis and power analysis at 12\,nm and 1\,GHz, then construct a chip-level throughput model under common area and power constraints. Five precision-migration scenarios represent possible changes in future workloads, allowing us to evaluate the estimated GEMM compute-latency benefits of nine throughput ratios.

Floating-point formats encode a sign, an exponent, and a fraction. The exponent width determines dynamic range, whereas the fraction width determines relative precision. TF32 retains FP32's exponent range with a shorter significand to reduce the cost of tensor computation; FP16 and BF16 favor precision and dynamic range, respectively~. The Open Compute Project (OCP) microscaling (MX) formats~ represent each element as $x_{j,i}=X_jP_{j,i}$, where $X_j$ is a shared block scaling factor and $P_{j,i}$ is the decoded element value. MXFP8, MXFP6, and MXFP4 use E5M2/E4M3, E3M2/E2M3, and E2M1 element encodings, respectively. All three share one E8M0 scale across 32 elements to extend the representable range.

TF32 retains FP32's exponent range with a shorter significand to reduce the cost of tensor computation; FP16 and BF16 favor precision and dynamic range, respectively~. The Open Compute Project (OCP) microscaling (MX) formats~ represent each element as $x_{j,i}=X_jP_{j,i}$, where $X_j$ is a shared block scaling factor and $P_{j,i}$ is the decoded element value. MXFP8, MXFP6, and MXFP4 use E5M2/E4M3, E3M2/E2M3, and E2M1 element encodings, respectively. All three share one E8M0 scale across 32 elements to extend the representable range.

HiF4 instead uses S1P2 fixed-point elements and hierarchical micro-exponent scaling to balance within-block dynamic range and precision~. \subsection{Group: Scale-Factor Integration and Unified Partial Sums}

Two Lanes form a T2H4Q8E16 Group, matching NVFP4's 16-element scaling block; larger blocks broadcast the same scale factor across Groups. The Group first combines the Lane results and separates the sign and magnitude, then applies the shared scale factors. Only NVFP4/HiF4 require scale-significand multiplication. The two four-bit scale significands are premultiplied into an eight-bit coefficient. After removing structurally zero low-order bits, the 14-bit Group magnitude is multiplied by this coefficient using a shared $14\times8$ multiplier. The resulting 22-bit value is mapped to the U31 magnitude interface. MX's E8M0 scale factors contribute only to the exponent.

Specialization preserves the numerical mappings, precision, and rounding rules of supported formats while removing decoding and arithmetic for unsupported formats. Each Lane in a Q8E16 Group uses eight $4\times4$ multipliers; Q activates four, whereas E activates all eight. It retains Q's 28-bit alignment path, the 31-bit Lane output, and E's scale-significand multiplication. Q8 retains only four $4\times4$ multipliers per Lane and removes E decoding, micro-exponent processing, and scale-significand multiplication. E8M0 scale factors contribute only to exponent updates.

E16 further reduces the alignment and reduction hardware. Each Lane retains eight $4\times4$ multipliers but removes element-exponent comparison, local alignment-reference generation across Lanes, and wide shifters. A narrow adder tree performs reduction, with HiF4's second-level micro-exponent incorporated after local summation; the Lane output is reduced to 14 signed bits. Combining two Lanes produces a 15-bit Group sum. Scaling and LZD operate on a 22-bit result, which is mapped to the common U31 magnitude and Anchor interface. E16 expansion therefore avoids the cost of Q's wide alignment and reduction paths.

Fig.~ shows the area and power of the nine configurations. \textbf{Expanding MXFP4 throughput incurs less area overhead than expanding MXFP8.} Relative to $1:2:4$, $1:2:8$ doubles MXFP4 throughput with only 33.60\% more area, whereas $1:4:8$ doubles both MXFP8 and MXFP4 throughput with 68.21\% more area. At higher ratios, $1:2:16$ and $1:8:16$ both provide four times the baseline MXFP4 throughput, but their area overheads are 83.68\% and 190.29\%, respectively. This difference reflects the lower cost of specialized MXFP4 datapaths, which omit portions of the exponent-comparison and alignment logic and use narrower reduction paths.

This difference reflects the lower cost of specialized MXFP4 datapaths, which omit portions of the exponent-comparison and alignment logic and use narrower reduction paths.
